title: Amazon's Anthropic Notes Are Worth $97.9 Billion as VCs Split Billions in IPO
excerpt: Anthropic's S-1 shows no venture firm even reaches 5%, while Amazon's convertible notes — $6.2 billion of principal — were valued at $97.9 billion before the listing.
body:
• Amazon is likely the single largest financial beneficiary of Anthropic's IPO: its $6.2 billion in convertible notes were valued at $97.9 billion on June 30, and its total investment is about $18 billion.
  • No venture firm owns the 5% needed to appear in the S-1's principal stockholders table — at a $965 billion private valuation, even Menlo's roughly $14 billion position is only about 1.5%.
  • Anthropic booked a $72.4 billion non-cash charge in the first half of 2026 just from the rising fair value of what it owes noteholders.
  • Google is the other giant winner: an estimated stake near 5.6% plus at least $114 billion in cloud commitments from Anthropic through 2033.

Many investors stand to win big when Anthropic goes public. Stakes held by Menlo Ventures, Sequoia, Sound Ventures and Spark Capital are expected to return billions. But according to Anthropic's S-1, none of those venture firms owns 5%, the threshold for inclusion in the principal stockholders' table — and the filing makes clear the biggest winner is not a venture firm at all, TechCrunch reported.

Why the VCs look small

The reason is Anthropic's size. At its $965 billion private valuation, a 1% stake is worth nearly $10 billion, so Menlo's roughly $14 billion position is only about 1.5% of the company, according to Bloomberg figures reported by TechCrunch. In a typical tech IPO, lead venture investors hold double-digit stakes; here, the sums are enormous and the percentages are not. Anthropic instead sold large stakes to strategic partners — companies that are also its business partners and, in Amazon's and Google's cases, the landlords of the computing power it runs on. We looked at the Indian-origin leaders inside the company in our coverage of Anthropic's road to a near-trillion-dollar listing.

Amazon's $18 billion bet, structured as debt

Amazon first backed Anthropic in 2023 with a commitment to invest up to $4 billion. Instead of taking stock upfront, it structured much of its investment as convertible notes — debt that converts into shares at an IPO or sale. According to the S-1, Amazon holds convertible notes with $6.2 billion in principal outstanding as of June 30, which is Anthropic's entire debt load. As Anthropic's valuation soared across successive funding rounds, the shares those notes will convert into became far more valuable: Amazon's own filings valued its note holdings at $97.9 billion as of June 30.

The notes could convert into as many as 1.84 billion shares, but a cap limits Amazon to 12% of Anthropic's "partially diluted" share count — a figure that counts some shares not yet issued, such as stock options. Amazon can waive the cap; notes that cannot convert stay outstanding and convert in later quarters under the same limit. Beyond the notes, Amazon invested $10 billion in nonvoting preferred stock in the second quarter — $5 billion in each of Anthropic's last two funding rounds — bringing its total investment to about $18 billion. And beyond the equity, Anthropic has committed to spend at least $110 billion on AWS over the next 10 years.

"The biggest winners of Anthropic's IPO may well be tech giants like Amazon, which backed a would-be rival early on and now sell it much of the computing power it runs on."

— TechCrunch, on Anthropic's S-1

The accounting bill for success

As the value of Amazon's notes surged, Anthropic had to record the growing value of what it owes. It reported the adjustments under "change in fair value of convertible notes, derivative liabilities, and SAFEs," a line that totaled $72.4 billion for the first half of 2026. The charge is non-cash — no money left the company — but it shows how a rising valuation can produce enormous paper losses for a company whose debt converts into its own ever-pricier shares. The Economic Times has separately flagged the open questions hanging over the record listing, from valuation to the strategic investors' competing interests.

Google's parallel windfall

Google, too, is set for a major gain. It held about 14% of Anthropic as of early last year, according to court filings reported by The New York Times, and has invested more since, including $10 billion in April. PitchBook analyst Harrison Rolfes told TechCrunch he estimates Google's current stake at closer to 5.6% after dilution. Google has also secured at least $114 billion in cloud commitments from Anthropic through 2033. The S-1 itself warns that some of those cloud providers also build rival AI models and may not always want the same things Anthropic does — a conflict public-market investors will have to price when the shares begin trading.
